# NetGuard IoT — Network Anomaly Detector with Auto-Generated ATT&CK Incident Reports

A working IoT network anomaly detection system with:

- **ML-based anomaly detection** (IsolationForest, unsupervised) on per-device traffic windows
- **Rule-based attack classification** (port scan, DDoS/botnet, brute force, C2 beaconing)
- **MITRE ATT&CK mapping** for every detected attack type
- **Auto-generated PDF incident reports** with timeline, evidence hashes, and recommended actions
- **MongoDB storage** for alerts and traffic logs (real Atlas cluster or local, with automatic in-memory fallback for offline demos)
- **Web dashboard** (Flask) to run simulations, view alerts, and download reports

This is designed to be presented as a working system to an examiner, and is
structured so each module can be explained and extended independently.

---

## Quick start (offline demo mode — no MongoDB needed)

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 1. Train the anomaly detection model (only needed once)
python3 -m ml.train_model

# 2. Start the web dashboard
python3 app.py

# 3. Open http://127.0.0.1:5000 in your browser
```

Click **"Run Simulation"** on the dashboard. This generates a batch of synthetic
IoT traffic (mostly normal, with a few injected attacks), runs it through the
full detection pipeline, and shows the resulting alerts. Click any alert to
see full details, and click **"Generate Incident Report"** to get a PDF with
the MITRE ATT&CK mapping.

Without a `MONGO_URI` environment variable set, the app automatically uses
`mongomock` (an in-memory MongoDB-compatible store) so you can demo the
entire system without needing a real database — useful for offline
presentations or marking sessions with no internet.

---

## Connecting a real MongoDB (cloud) database

1. Create a free cluster at [MongoDB Atlas](https://www.mongodb.com/cloud/atlas)
2. Get your connection string (Database → Connect → Drivers), e.g.:
   ```
   mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@cluster0.xxxxx.mongodb.net/
   ```
3. Set it as an environment variable before running the app:
   ```bash
   export MONGO_URI="mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@cluster0.xxxxx.mongodb.net/"
   python3 app.py
   ```
4. The dashboard header will show `Storage backend: REAL` once connected.
   All alerts and traffic logs will now persist in your Atlas cluster,
   visible from MongoDB Compass or the Atlas web UI too.

No code changes are needed to switch between modes — `storage/mongo_client.py`
handles the detection and fallback automatically.

---

## Architecture

```
traffic/                    <- Where traffic data comes from (3 interchangeable sources)
  synthetic_generator.py    <- Demo/training data generator (used in this sandbox)
  pcap_reader.py            <- Reads a real .pcap file (Wireshark/tcpdump capture)
  live_capture.py           <- Live sniffing with scapy (run on a real interface, needs root)
  feature_extraction.py     <- Shared: raw packets -> feature vector

ml/
  train_model.py            <- Trains IsolationForest on normal traffic, saves to models/
  detector.py                <- Loads model, scores a traffic window -> anomaly score

intelligence/
  rule_classifier.py         <- Classifies WHICH attack type an anomaly looks like
  attack_mapping.json         <- Rule table: attack type -> MITRE ATT&CK technique

storage/
  mongo_client.py             <- MongoDB connection (real Atlas or mongomock fallback)
  alert_store.py               <- Insert/query alerts + traffic logs

forensics/
  report_template.html         <- Jinja2 + CSS template for the PDF report
  generate_report.py            <- Renders + hashes the PDF from a stored alert

pipeline.py                    <- Orchestrates: detect -> classify -> map -> score -> store
app.py                          <- Flask web dashboard
templates/, static/             <- Dashboard HTML + CSS
models/                          <- Saved ML model + scaler (generated by train_model.py)
output/reports/                  <- Generated PDF incident reports land here
```

### Data flow

```
Traffic source (synthetic / pcap / live)
        |
        v
feature_extraction.py  --> feature vector (packet rate, port entropy, syn ratio, etc.)
        |
        v
ml/detector.py  --> anomaly_score + is_anomaly (IsolationForest)
        |
        v (only if anomalous)
intelligence/rule_classifier.py  --> attack_type (e.g. "ddos_traffic")
        |
        v
intelligence/attack_mapping.json  --> MITRE ATT&CK technique + recommended actions
        |
        v
storage/alert_store.py  --> stored in MongoDB (alerts + traffic_logs collections)
        |
        v (on demand, from dashboard)
forensics/generate_report.py  --> PDF incident report, SHA-256 hashed
```

---

## Using real network traffic instead of synthetic data

The synthetic generator (`traffic/synthetic_generator.py`) exists because this
was built in a sandboxed environment with no live network interface. For your
actual course deployment, you have two real options that plug into the exact
same pipeline with no other code changes:

### Option A — Analyze a captured pcap file
```bash
python3 -c "
from traffic.pcap_reader import read_pcap_windows
from pipeline import run_batch

windows = read_pcap_windows('your_capture.pcap', window_seconds=10.0)
alert_ids = run_batch(windows)
print('Alerts created:', alert_ids)
"
```
Capture a `.pcap` with Wireshark or `tcpdump -w capture.pcap` on your IoT VLAN,
then run the above.

### Option B — Live capture (run on a lab machine / Raspberry Pi with root)
```bash
sudo python3 traffic/live_capture.py --iface eth0 --window 10
```
Wire `LiveWindowCollector`'s `on_window_ready` callback to call
`pipeline.run_batch()` directly for real-time detection (see the docstring
in `traffic/live_capture.py`).

---

## Extending the project

- **Add more attack types**: add a new rule to `intelligence/rule_classifier.py`
  and a matching entry to `intelligence/attack_mapping.json` — no other
  changes needed.
- **Improve attack classification with ML instead of rules**: once you have
  labeled data, you could train a supervised classifier (e.g., Random Forest)
  to replace `rule_classifier.py` — the interface (`features -> alert_type`)
  stays the same.
- **Device fingerprinting**: add a classifier that identifies device
  type/vendor from traffic patterns, and pass richer `device` dicts into
  the pipeline (already has fields for `vendor`, `type` — just populate
  them from your fingerprinting model instead of the synthetic generator).
- **Live MITRE data**: replace the hardcoded descriptions in
  `attack_mapping.json` with live lookups from MITRE's public STIX dataset
  (`mitre-attack/attack-stix-data` on GitHub) for always-current technique text.
- **Real evidence capture**: `pipeline._build_evidence()` currently hashes a
  JSON summary of the packet list as a stand-in. In a real deployment, save
  the actual pcap segment for the flagged window to disk (or cloud storage)
  and hash that file instead.

---

## Notes on the ML approach (for your report/viva)

- **IsolationForest** is trained only on **normal** traffic (unsupervised
  novelty detection) — this reflects reality, since labeled attack traffic
  is scarce and attackers constantly invent new patterns. The model learns
  "what normal looks like" and flags anything sufficiently different.
- **Rule-based attack classification** is used *after* the ML model flags
  something anomalous, to determine *what kind* of attack it resembles.
  This two-stage design (ML for detection, rules for attribution) mirrors
  real-world security tools and is fully explainable — every classification
  can be traced to a specific threshold check, which is much easier to
  defend in a viva than a black-box multi-class classifier.
- **Severity scoring** combines the ML anomaly score with each ATT&CK
  technique's inherent severity weight:
  `combined = (anomaly_score * 0.6) + (attack_severity_weight * 0.4)`
